item.title: Markov-Shielded Typicality for Thermal Quantum States
item.description: arXiv:2611.10593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pure states of quantum many-body systems at thermal equilibrium are known to be typical, in a sense that a randomly chosen pure state from an appropriate energy shell reproduces the Gibbs-state expectation values of most observables acting on a small subsystem. However, such typical states are intrinsically stochastic, conventionally generated from the random high-temperature state, suffer from statistical fluctuations, and do not provide a continuous connection to the ground state. Here, we introduce a deterministic variational framework for constructing a Markov-Shielded Typical (MST) state, a unique thermal pure-state representative whose local reduced density matrices closely approximate those of the Gibbs state, from the ground state up to infinite-temperature limit. Our approach reformulates free-energy minimization by replacing the nonlocal von Neumann entropy with a local, computationally tractable Markov entropy, where we establish rigorous upper and lower bounds of MST free energy to lie in the very vicinity of the thermal free energy. This framework extends the concept of typicality to deterministic pure-state representations of thermal equilibrium, offering a scalable wave-function approach with potential applications to both classical and quantum computing.
item.dc:creator: Atsushi Iwaki, Chisa Hotta

item.title: Dynamic Scaling and Aging in Hydrodynamic Coarsening of Vapor Bubbles in a Lennard-Jones Fluid
item.description: arXiv:2611.10621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the coarsening and aging dynamics of vapor bubbles during liquid-vapor phase separation in a three-dimensional single-component Lennard-Jones fluid using large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Following a temperature quench from a homogeneous high-temperature state into the two-phase coexistence region, vapor bubbles nucleate and grow in the liquid background. The characteristic bubble size follows a power-law growth, $\ell(t)\sim t^\alpha$, with a growth exponent $\alpha \simeq 2/3$, characteristic of inertial hydrodynamic coarsening. We also investigate the two-time autocorrelation function $C_{ag}(t,t_w)$ which follows waiting-time dependent relaxation, revealing aging. Furthermore, data at different waiting times collapse onto a scaling function when plotted as a function of the length ratio $\ell(t)/\ell(t_w)$, demonstrating dynamical scaling during aging. The corresponding scaling function exhibits an algebraic decay with an exponent $\lambda \simeq 3$. Interestingly, bubble and droplet growth exhibit distinctly different domain-growth and aging exponents despite both being disconnected morphologies.
item.dc:creator: Sutapa Roy

item.title: Ising model on Calandre lattice
item.description: arXiv:2611.10834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we proposed to consideration a noval (not yet exploited) planar lattice --- Calandre lattice with the Ising model applied to it. In the framework of an exact analytical Kramers--Wannier transfer-matrix approach and using an extension of the combinatorial Vdovichenko--Feynman method, we have obtained exact solution for Helmholtz free energy and consequent expression for the principal eigenvalue of the Kramers--Wannier transfer-matrix. In addition, we derived the exact expression for spontaneous magnetization. The usage of both expressions made it possible to perform the comprehensive studies of thermodynamic and magnetic properties of the Calandre lattice itself and a wide variety of its affiliated lattices. Among them, diversified interrelations between Calandre lattice and already known and even some novel lattices. These lattices have also revealed such effects as magnetic frustrations, multiple phase transitions and magnetic reentrancy.
item.dc:creator: F. A. Kassan-Ogly, A. V. Zarubin

item.title: Ergotropy as distance from equilibrium
item.description: arXiv:2611.11343v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the ergotropy (a.k.a available energy) of a thermally isolated system is the $1$-Wasserstein distance between two energy probability density functions. Specifically, between the energy profile of the system state, and the energy profile of its associated passive state. We prove this for both classical and quantum systems, and illustrate it with examples. Our result formalises the intuition that ergotropy is a quantifier of distance from equilibrium
item.dc:creator: Michele Campisi

item.title: Computing Classical Partition Functions via Cycle-Space Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2611.11850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a method for computing thermodynamic properties of classical spin systems by reformulating the partition function as a sum over even subgraphs of the interaction graph. Starting from the high-temperature expansion, we show that the expansion coefficients are determined by the weight distribution of the null space of the binary incidence matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and that this statement holds verbatim for multi-spin interactions once the graph is replaced by a hypergraph. We introduce a Monte Carlo scheme based on the $1/t$ Wang-Landau algorithm that performs a random walk directly in this null space. Because the weight distribution is temperature independent, a single estimate yields the zero-field partition function, and the thermodynamic quantities obtained from its temperature derivatives, at arbitrary temperature. We validate the approach against exact finite-size results on the two-dimensional triangular-lattice Ising model, apply it to the three- and four-dimensional hypercubic Ising models where no exact solution is available, and to the two- and three-dimensional Baxter-Wu models, whose three-spin interactions place them outside the reach of Pfaffian methods. For the two-body models we compare against conventional Wang-Landau sampling in energy space; for the Baxter-Wu models we validate against exact enumeration at the smallest size in each dimension.
item.dc:creator: Yoav Feigenbaum, Lev Barash, Itay Hen

item.title: The role of preparation protocols in the Mpemba effect under time-delayed Newton cooling
item.description: arXiv:2611.12328v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mpemba effect depends on both the relaxation dynamics and the protocol used to prepare the initial states. Here, this dependence is investigated using the time-delayed Newton cooling law, comparing protocols in which two samples are exposed to piecewise-constant bath temperatures before being placed in a common final bath. For protocols with at most two quenches and a common waiting time, exact conditions for the occurrence of the effect are derived. They rule out the Pontus protocol within this model and show that the synchronous two-reservoir protocol maximizes the effect magnitude within the class considered. The robustness of this optimum is then examined by allowing asynchronous quenches or an additional quench for one sample. Numerical optimization of these extensions identifies the synchronous two-reservoir protocol as the maximizing limit in the cases studied. This evidence motivates a conjecture that the same protocol remains optimal for more general bath histories, although that broader statement is not proved.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'es Santos

item.title: Discrete time crystals stabilized by bounded measurement noise
item.description: arXiv:2611.12400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodically driven clean interacting systems generically heat up, which destroys discrete time-crystalline order. Here we ask whether continuous weak measurement can stabilize such order. We study a long-range interacting spin chain whose local occupation is continuously monitored. Measurements generally induce a transition from volume-law to area-law entanglement. Yet low entanglement alone is not enough: along typical quantum trajectories, the system still reaches a featureless state with no subharmonic response. In contrast, the most-probable trajectory, obtained by suppressing measurement fluctuations, shows robust period doubling. To connect these limits, we introduce a bounded-noise protocol that restricts measurement fluctuations to a finite window. Narrow windows preserve period doubling. Intermediate windows produce coexisting time-crystalline and non-time-crystalline trajectories. Over time, trajectories leave the time-crystalline group one by one, so the order is long lived but finite. Wide windows destroy the order. Our results establish bounded measurement noise, discarding the large-deviation trajectories, as a route to time-crystalline order in clean systems. They also show that the measurement-induced area-law phase is necessary, but not sufficient, for this order.
item.dc:creator: Pallabi Chatterjee, Tanay Nag, Ranjan Modak

item.title: Deriving Tsallis Entropy from First Principles
item.description: arXiv:2611.12441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The kinetic approach for q-distribution is extended through a "bottom-up" procedure to the corresponding entropic formula. In this way, the validity of Tsallis' formula, S_q(W) = k_B ln_q(W), is established from first principles. The resulting q-entropy is additive and the zeroth law of thermodynamics is automatically satisfied because the conventional identification beta = 1/(k_B T) remains valid. Entropy, energy, and all relevant quantities for both discrete and continuous cases are evaluated using standard (linear) averages. The "bottom-up" and "top-down" approaches yield the same q-distribution for velocities. The standard results are naturally recovered in the limit q -> 1.
item.dc:creator: J. A. S. Lima, M. H. Benetti

item.title: Giant Diffusion at Flocking Transitions
item.description: arXiv:2611.12465v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We simulate dynamics in two-dimensional aligning active-matter models exhibiting order-disorder transitions in the velocity field. Analysis reveals that the single-particle diffusivity, $D_s$, exhibits strong enhancements at criticality which we quantify via a finite-size scaling method. This dynamical behavior at nonequilibrium flocking transitions is fundamentally different from that at the criticality of equilibrium systems, where diffusivities either vanish or remain non-critical. Furthermore, $D_s$ exhibits pronounced finite-size effects throughout the ordered phase, which also are absent in equilibrium settings. We interpret these counterintuitive transport anomalies within the framework of a flocking theory. Our results suggest that enhanced diffusion generates effective long-range interactions. This relaxes the constraints of the Mermin-Wagner theorem that otherwise prevents order-disorder transitions in two dimensions for systems possessing continuous symmetry. These results are of much experimental relevance and have important implications in formulating quantitative theories for nonequilibrium transports.
item.dc:creator: Sohini Chatterjee, Wasim Akram, Subir K. Das

item.title: Holonomy, Spectral Topology, and Detailed Balance in Classical and Open Quantum Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.12514v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Band topology and non-Hermitian spectral theory are now applied to mechanical metamaterials, chiral active fluids, stochastic networks, and open quantum systems. We give a tutorial synthesis organized by holonomy and by one question: what can the spectral data of a linear generator reveal about detailed balance? Three holonomies recur: the Berry phase of a band, the Burgers vector of a dislocation (the integrated torsion of the defect geometry), and the cycle affinity of a Markov network (the holonomy of the connection $\ln(W_{ij}/W_{ji})$). We rederive the Chern numbers $C_m=m(\mathrm{sgn}\,\Omega+\mathrm{sgn}\,\nu_o)$ of a compressible odd-viscous fluid and restate the dislocation zero-mode count of Paulose, Chen, and Vitelli as a pairing of integrated torsion with topological polarization. Our central message is that spectral topology can obstruct detailed balance but does not determine the magnitude of dissipation. Detailed balance is self-adjointness in the inner product fixed by the stationary state, so a non-real eigenvalue, an exceptional point (EP), or a nonzero point-gap winding number of a Markov generator rules it out and forces entropy production $\sigma>0$, with $\sigma\ge k_B j^2/D$ for any current, whereas a real, diagonalizable spectrum does not in general certify it. In the Hatano-Nelson ring, which is normal yet has complex spectrum, $\sigma$ sweeps $(0,\infty)$ at fixed winding number. EPs need a separate assessment of the dynamics: with generalized detailed balance including time-reversal parity, an EP is compatible with equilibrium only through time-reversal-odd dynamics, as at critical damping of a Langevin oscillator, whereas an EP of a system with only even variables, such as an odd elastic medium, certifies a nonequilibrium steady state; in both cases $\sigma$ is analytic across the EP. We propose benchtop tests for each statement.
item.dc:creator: Alvan Hunt

item.title: Memory in biological L\'evy walks from the dynamic-entropy formalism
item.description: arXiv:2611.12547v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: L\'evy walks are recognized by the histogram of their flight lengths, while the renewal hypothesis on which the textbook model rests, that every flight is drawn afresh, is seldom tested. We test it with the dynamic-entropy formalism. Maximizing the causal entropy of a sequence of logarithmic flight lengths at fixed lagged correlations yields a chain of continuous spins on a compact interval, whose depth, selected by the data, tells a renewal walker from a Markovian one and from one with a longer memory. With one lag the chain is exactly solvable. A duality that exchanges long and short flights locates a first-order condensation of the flights at the upper cutoff, with the logarithmic range of the flights in the role of system size, and a positive memory makes the histogram heavier-tailed than the rule that generates each flight. For groups, the same construction separates the memory of each individual from delayed interactions and from drives common to all units, which an analysis of the group average confounds, and it gives the collective speed a critical point. On open data, renewal is rejected in seven of ten conditions of Drosophila larvae and in every termite, whose memory reaches a few flights back and lowers the exponent of the histogram by more than half a unit below that of the one-step rule. Wild baboons align with where their nearest neighbors, those ahead above all, were heading 10 to 30 s earlier, and homing pigeons are coupled across their small flocks. Zebrafish T cells, a negative control, remember their own speed, but no delayed coupling between the speeds of different cells survives the controls.
item.dc:creator: Adriano Barra, Andrea Ladiana

item.title: Resolving the backbone of multiscale interactions through mutual information rates
item.description: arXiv:2611.12554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural systems are often composed of processes evolving on multiple timescales and coupled through complex interaction networks. Inferring such networks is especially challenging when timescales are widely separated, since resolving the fastest processes while accurately sampling the slowest ones is generally prohibitive. In this work, we propose a framework to reconstruct a multiscale interaction tree by combining a rescaled version of the mutual information rate, its conditional counterpart, and the ordering of timescales. We derive an exact theory for stationary Gaussian processes, finding that these measures identify directly connected processes, with the asymptotic mutual information rate distinguishing fast-to-slow from slow-to-fast couplings. We show that this reconstruction can be achieved from the spectral matrix and illustrate its robustness to finite trajectory lengths, moderate timescale separation, and weak nonlinearities. Our work paves the way for exploiting the presence of multiple timescales in real-world systems as a source of structural identifiability rather than an obstacle to network inference.
item.dc:creator: Alberto Raiola, Giorgio Nicoletti, Daniel Maria Busiello

item.title: A Hierarchy of Fast and Strong Signatures for Vertex Orbits
item.description: arXiv:2611.12653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The defining features of a physical system are its symmetries and its invariants. For a network, the symmetries are the automorphisms, and the invariants are the vertex orbits they define. Two vertices of a graph may appear structurally indistinguishable without being interchangeable under any graph automorphism. Distinguishing apparent similarity from genuine symmetry lies at the heart of the vertex-orbit partition problem. In this work, we develop a hierarchy of increasingly expressive, automorphism-invariant signatures that draw on the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian and the Dirac operator to reveal subtle structural differences. Guided by a sequence of counterexamples, we progressively strengthen these signatures, ultimately incorporating probing techniques, which are temporary structural perturbations, that expose the hidden distinctions in the original unperturbed graph. We evaluate our approach across diverse benchmark families, recovering exact orbit partitions in challenging instances, including graphs that resist low-dimensional Weisfeiler--Leman refinement. We also examine the computational and numerical limitations of our constructions, distinguishing empirical success from theoretical completeness. Our findings highlight the potential of spectral and probing-based methods for uncovering the structural distinctions that define vertex orbit.
item.dc:creator: Joe Germany, Mohamad Al Sayed, Rana Dbouk, Amer E. Mouawad, Sara Najem

item.title: Renewal Bias in Parallel Simulations of Absorbing Processes
item.description: arXiv:2611.12692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous parallel simulations of stochastic processes with absorbing states can exhibit systematic sampling bias when trajectory durations depend on their eventual absorbing outcomes. Workers that continuously restart upon absorption preferentially record rapidly terminating trajectories within a fixed computational budget, distorting the observed ensemble statistics. We investigate this effect using a minimal renewal model with two absorbing states and state-dependent exponential durations. Renewal theory yields exact expressions for the expected number and composition of completed trajectories, showing that the resulting bias decreases algebraically with execution time but persists as the number of parallel workers increases at fixed budget. We compare continuous sampling with First-Trajectory Filtering, which retains only the initial trajectory attempted by each worker. Although finite execution deadlines introduce residual censoring bias, this bias decreases exponentially with the computational budget. An analytical mean-squared error calculation reveals budget-dependent crossover worker allocations beyond which First-Trajectory Filtering becomes more accurate despite collecting fewer trajectories. We also examine the limitations of statistical inference under severe censoring when the absorbing-state probabilities and characteristic durations are unknown. Finally, simulations of the Axelrod model near its nonequilibrium transition demonstrate the preferential sampling of rapidly absorbing fragmented configurations, illustrating the relevance of the renewal mechanism in a spatially interacting system. Our results show that increasing computational throughput does not necessarily improve statistical accuracy and highlight the importance of accounting for trajectory-duration heterogeneity in parallel simulations of absorbing processes.
item.dc:creator: Sandro M. Reia, Jos\'e F. Fontanari

item.title: Prestatability in the Macroscopic Limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.09989v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We examine whether the variables required for a future macroscopic description of a given physical system can themselves be stated in advance. Representing macroscopic descriptions as coarse-grainings of a fixed microscopic phase space, we distinguish formal prestatability, concerning the existence of an effective complete vocabulary of admissible macroscopic distinctions, from dynamical prestatability, concerning whether the future relevance of those distinctions is decidable. Both obstructions disappear for finite microscopic state spaces. In the infinite limit, exhaustive formal prestatability can fail, while a restricted predictive architecture may remain formally pre-statable. We construct such an architecture and show that, under universal dynamics, the future relevance of a candidate variable is equivalent to the halting problem. Thus a fixed microscopic phase space can support macroscopic descriptions whose future variables are not fully pre-statable.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Palessandro

item.title: Efficient classical simulation of Fermi-Hubbard models with Kramers symmetry
item.description: arXiv:2611.10039v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum Monte Carlo methods are widely used to solve quantum many-body problems. However, rigorous guarantees for their performance are poorly understood, especially for simulating interacting fermions. In this work, we develop a quantum Monte Carlo algorithm for a broad family of fermionic systems exhibiting Kramers time-reversal symmetry, and prove that their partition functions can be estimated in polynomial time. This family, which contains many important classes of Hubbard-type models, is known to both avoid the sign problem and obey a Lee-Yang zero-freeness theorem. Thus our results suggest that these two properties together may enable efficient classical algorithms for quantum many-body systems more broadly.
item.dc:creator: Chaithanya Rayudu, Jun Takahashi, Ojas Parekh, Andrew Zhao

item.title: Learning the interactions underlying multicellular migration using many-body stochastic inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.10138v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Uncovering the interactions that give rise to emergent collective behavior in active and living matter remains a major challenge. Multicellular migration exemplifies this challenge: complex cell-cell interactions shape collective motion, but are difficult to measure directly. Here, we introduce a many-body stochastic inference framework that learns these interactions directly from experimental trajectories. We infer interaction models spanning different dynamical dependencies and complexities from short-time cell dynamics, and select among them based on their ability to predict emergent collective behaviors. Applied across three behaviorally distinct cell types, this approach yields minimal, predictive models of cell-cell interactions underlying multicellular migration. We find that non-cancerous epithelial cells coordinate multicellular migration through reciprocal repulsion and velocity alignment, while cancerous mesenchymal cells additionally exhibit previously unrecognized nonreciprocal interactions that couple to self-propulsion through two distinct mechanisms, which we term velocity inhibition in fibrosarcoma cells and velocity enhancement in breast cancer cells. Conceptually, these nonreciprocal interactions allow cells to tune the onset and speed of flocks, underscoring their role in collective migration and potentially enhancing cancer cell invasiveness at large cell densities. More broadly, our framework offers a general and principled route for extracting interaction laws of active and living systems directly from data.
item.dc:creator: Bram J. Hoogland, Tom Brandst\"atter, Emily Brieger, Joachim O. R\"adler, Chase P. Broedersz

item.title: The satisfiability conjecture for random k-SAT formulas. Human-friendly exposition of the recent OpenAI resolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.10139v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The satisfiability conjecture was one of the most important open problems in discrete probability. It was resolved recently first by Carenini~\cite{GCarenini}, and shortly after by OpenAI~\cite{k-sat-OpenAI}, among other 370 problems solved by its internal model. The conjecture concerned the satisfiability property of random instances of the k-SAT problem. It posits the existence of a fixed value for the clause-to-variables ratio around which the probability that the formula is satisfiable drops sharply from nearly one to nearly zero as the ratio increases. While the case of large constant $k$ was resolved a decade ago by Ding, Sly and Sun~\cite{ding2015proof,ding2022proof} using the heavy machinery of the second moment method, the case of general $k$ eluded proof until ~\cite{GCarenini} and~\cite{k-sat-OpenAI}. In this short note we provide a ''human-friendly'' and detailed exposition of the OpenAI's resolution of the conjecture.
item.dc:creator: David Gamarnik

item.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2611.10338v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.
item.dc:creator: Defang Chen, Zhenyu Zhou, Can Wang, Zeyu Zheng, Siwei Lyu

item.title: Is price-impact decay statistically identifiable by propagator estimation? Diffusive prices force the inferred kernel to be transient and fine-tuned
item.description: arXiv:2611.10574v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Despite the long memory of market-order flow, price dynamics remain diffusive---a seemingly paradoxical coexistence known in econophysics as the diffusivity puzzle. The propagator model has long been regarded as a promising solution: price impact decays in time, finely balanced against the order-flow memory, and propagators inferred from data have been reported to be consistent with this fine balance. Here we prove a no-go theorem: asymptotic impact decay is not statistically identifiable by propagator estimation, since for diffusive prices the fine-tuned decay is returned whether or not the true impact decays. It rests on universal theorems for the Wiener--Hopf deconvolution by which propagators are inferred under long-memory order flow: (i) the inferred propagator is necessarily transient, even when the true impact is permanent; (ii) under a mild condition, it decays with the fine-balance exponent, fixed by the order-flow autocorrelation alone. The fine-tuned decay is thus a property of the deconvolution, not evidence of impact decay. We demonstrate this with an exactly solvable null model that retains order splitting and the square-root law but whose impact is strictly permanent: the inferred propagator shows an artificial fine-tuned decay although the true impact never decays. Nonlinear propagator estimation, being of Wiener--Hopf type, is subject to the same theorems whenever true metaorders have long memory.
item.dc:creator: Shunta Fujiwara, Yuki Sato, Kiyoshi Kanazawa

item.title: Hyperuniformity in active matter
item.description: arXiv:2611.10605v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Disordered hyperuniform systems are characterized by an anomalously strong suppression of long-wavelength density fluctuations. As a result, these unusual materials behave as though virtually incompressible, even though the particle arrangement itself can remain fully disordered at short range. This peculiar state of matter has been the topic of intense research in physics and mathematics in recent years. Another flourishing research arena is active matter, composed of self-propelled agents that convert energy into motion. While the two fields remained largely disjunct for a long time, the paper by Lei and coworkers (2019) created a link between hyperuniformity and active matter by demonstrating that interacting circle swimmers self-organize into disordered hyperuniform structures. Inspired by this work, many other examples of hyperuniformity in active matter have been identified. We shall describe the impact and outgrowth of this development, and give a brief perspective on further links between hyperuniformity and active matter.
item.dc:creator: Hartmut L\"owen, Erdal C. O\u{g}uz

item.title: Strong Collective Dynamics Hidden behind a Nearly Free Single-Particle Spectrum
item.description: arXiv:2611.10636v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Single-particle spectroscopy has long served as a criterion for the strength of electronic correlations: strong collective motion is expected to shift and broaden spectral peaks and to renormalize the dispersion. Here we show that this correspondence can fail on the same microscopic orbital. The mechanism relies on local interference between two resonant side orbitals: one suppresses low-energy real transitions into the interacting environment, while the other suppresses spectral-weight backflow to the source orbital; virtual mixing nevertheless transfers the environmental spin polarization to the source. We prove a rigorous relative spectral bound that is uniform in environment size and interaction strength and holds for arbitrary stationary states; the protection becomes stronger as the relative frequency resolution improves. In a fully quantum two-cell device, a collective mode softens by 60%, whereas the particle intensity at the free peak changes by only 3.6 parts per million. Quantum Monte Carlo shows that the transferred spin response grows with spatial correlations and is quantitatively predicted by the free-band polarization. These results recast the meaning of a simple particle spectrum and provide a design principle for quantum probes that combine predictable particle spectra with strong collective sensitivity.
item.dc:creator: Zhixuan Zhao, Sicheng He, Hanxiang Di, Nayun Chen, Jiabai Xiong, Guyixue Gao, Yanling Wu, Jun Li

item.title: Monodromy Defects and Bulk Renormalization Group Flows on the Fuzzy Sphere
item.description: arXiv:2611.10815v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A monodromy around a defect specifies a symmetry transformation, but the low energy properties of the defect depend on its interaction with bulk degrees of freedom and also itself. We study this dependence on the fuzzy sphere. Along an anisotropy flow, an $O(3)$ half-twist approaches the $O(2)$ half-twist when its twisted components stay light and disappears when they become massive. At large $N$, untwisted spectators give a positive correction to the defect entropy, fixed by the conformal weight of the free defect. The surviving $O(2)$ monodromy admits a relevant charged perturbation that pins the line. Pinning before or after the easy-plane bulk flow gives matching infrared junction data. A pin of the untwisted component survives only the opposite, easy-axis flow. Walls between opposite pinnings test the stability of the candidate ordered line. They are relevant on the pinned $O(2)$ monodromy lines studied and favoured to be relevant, with a smaller margin, on the ordinary $O(2)$ line, while the ordinary $O(3)$ and $O(4)$ walls lie close to marginality. We separate the wall dimension into a tilt stiffness and an angular shape, comparing them with a Ward identity, a two-loop expansion and a large-$N$ saddle. In the fully twisted large-$N$ model, winding weakens the condensate and lowers the wall dimension and the entropy released by pinning. The resulting entropy comparison permits disordering into the unpinned line wherever the leading wall estimate is relevant. Finally, we construct the regular half-twist on the fuzzy four-sphere as a starting point for analogous questions in five dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Kimyeong Lee, Joydeep Naskar

item.title: One Measurement, Many Fronts in Kitaev and Cluster Chains
item.description: arXiv:2611.10912v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A projective measurement of one site in the ground state of a quantum chain disturbs the chain in two ways: learning the outcome shifts distant expectation values at once, through ground-state correlations, and the measurement erases the correlations between the measured site and the rest. Both changes travel outward. We solve this problem exactly for the Kitaev chain, the cluster chain in a transverse field, and the Kitaev chain with power-law couplings, and we find that far from the measured site every quadratic observable responds through a front. Where the front is and how fast it broadens depend only on the quasiparticle dispersion. How strong it is depends on two operators: how strongly the measured one creates the fastest quasiparticles and how strongly the observed one detects them; if either factor vanishes, the front is weaker and decays faster. One measurement therefore launches many fronts, one per observable, with a common position and width but different decay laws. In the Kitaev chain the density and the bond energy, the two terms of its nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian, respond to one density measurement with decay laws that trade places between the topological and the trivial phase; in the cluster chain, measuring a symmetry-odd spin instead of a symmetry-even one changes the critical decay law at a fixed Hamiltonian; and with power-law couplings the width law itself changes. All decay laws and profiles are obtained in closed form.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Musat, Stephan Haas, Rishabh Jha

item.title: Odd Darcy Law: Odd Viscosity and Edge Currents in Porous Media
item.description: arXiv:2611.11138v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We derive and numerically validate an odd Darcy law for chiral active fluids in porous media, in which an antisymmetric permeability tensor induces a flow transverse to the applied pressure gradient. We identify two distinct mechanisms leading to this odd response: odd viscosity in the fluid or the nonlinear coupling of edge currents to inertia. We then show how the transverse transport depends on porosity, boundary friction, and chirality.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Maire, Ignacio Pagonabarraga

item.title: Quantum entanglement as a resource for self-organization and stabilization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11175v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can quantum entanglement generate macroscopic order that persists after the entanglement itself disappears? We establish such a mechanism in a driven-dissipative bosonic lattice, where local entanglement enables transport that amplifies spatial fluctuations into extended Turing patterns. For the full nonlinear dynamics with noise and disorder, we derive rigorous finite-time bounds on pattern intensity for all admissible separable evolutions, allowing arbitrary classical correlations. Quantum dynamics produces pattern intensities beyond these bounds during both formation and stabilization under noise. The excess intensity also provides a lower bound on the accumulated transport contribution beyond the separable limit. We further introduce an environment that responds to emerging order by suppressing local coherence and activating classical transport. The patterns then persist as local entanglement is lost, with both stages arising from a single time-independent Lindblad equation. These results show how transient quantum resources can establish persistent macroscopic order, opening new directions for harnessing self-organization in nonequilibrium systems.
item.dc:creator: Kazuki Ikeda

item.title: Liberation in the Heavy Limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.11594v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study CFT four-point functions of identical scalar primaries as their dimension $\Delta$ grows for fixed $0<z, \bar z<1$, and call them liberated if they grow at the same exponential rate as those of a generalized free field (GFF), as is the case for heavy free particles propagating along geodesics in AdS. We show that the correlator is liberated at the crossing symmetric point if and only if the light spectrum is sparse, and that liberation then holds wherever $z$ and $\bar z$ lie on the same side of $1/2$. If the low twist states are also sparse, liberation holds everywhere except in an explicit band around $z+\bar z=1$. In particular, if the primary twist gap lies above $\sqrt{2}\Delta$, then the correlator is liberated everywhere. For twist cutoffs below $\Delta$, composites of two spinning generalized free fields fail to be liberated in a region that fills the band near the double lightcone limit. In two dimensions, Virasoro primaries cannot be liberated unless the central charge grows faster than $\Delta$. The same framework sharpens the universality of large-$c$ torus partition functions of two-dimensional CFTs.
item.dc:creator: Sridip Pal, Gordon Rogelberg

item.title: How Path Integral Diffusion Decides a Finite Spin Glass
item.description: arXiv:2611.11826v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When an AI diffusion-type generator samples a frustrated spin glass, which macroscopic alternatives does it decide first, and when? We study this for bridge-diffusion models of the Path Integral Diffusion (PID) type started from a point source. We show that every isotropic PID is a time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, and conversely every signal-to-noise schedule is realized by a PID protocol. What a continuous-time generator decides therefore does not depend on the protocol, which only sets when and at what cost. We describe the generator's state by its partial commitments: the probabilities it assigns, at each moment, to nested classes of configurations fixed by the target. The partial commitments are martingales that move only along class contrasts. Their ensemble average gives the information about each level at an exact rate set by squared magnetization contrasts. Each split is decided, approximately, like a binary Gaussian channel at signal-to-noise ratio 1.04/\lambda_P, with \lambda_P the leading eigenvalue of the parent's correlation matrix. The theory is applied to Bethe-lattice and Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) glasses with up to 64 spins. It is observed generically that a trajectory first shifts its weight to one of the two mirror halves of the zero-field measure and then to the glassy classes inside it. These classes appear near the glass transition and keep their identity on cooling. Nested glassy levels have similar \lambda_P and are decided together, so a trajectory commits in one or two distinct events---the mirror choice and a compound glassy decision---which separate further with coupling and size, as the spectra predict. For a generator that takes finitely many steps, the protocol matters through the late, local stage rather than the macroscopic decisions.
item.dc:creator: Michael Chertkov

item.title: Matrix-vector models for the 3D Ising CFT
item.description: arXiv:2611.12071v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The construction of three-dimensional conformal field theories (3D CFTs) using interacting fermions in the lowest Landau level on a sphere has recently proven remarkably efficient, while it differs from that of conventional field theories on the fuzzy sphere. Focusing on the 3D Ising CFT, we consider a class of models that are defined by deformed Hamiltonians specified by a function which controls how the interaction is damped at high angular momenta, and this class includes the original model. We show that each model in the class can be reformulated in a basis-independent manner as a matrix--vector quantum-mechanical model, and, upon integrating out the fermionic vectors, as a matrix model. We then focus on a Gaussian choice, for which the bosonic matrices acquire a heat-kernel propagator whose width is controlled by a parameter $\xi$. Through exact diagonalization with the number of fermions up to $16$, we find that the low-energy spectra of the deformed Hamiltonians at criticality agree with those in the 3D Ising CFT for a range of $\xi$. We thus obtain matrix-model realizations of the 3D Ising CFT that, in contrast to conventional fuzzy-sphere field theories, show no sign of UV/IR mixing in the low-lying spectrum.
item.dc:creator: Kaichi Mizohata, Tatsuya Seko, Asato Tsuchiya

item.title: Linear response in generalized Lotka--Volterra systems with a finite number of species
item.description: arXiv:2611.12074v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding how species interactions shape ecosystem responses to perturbations is a central challenge in ecology. Random matrix theory (RMT) has been widely used to predict the responses of large random ecosystems, but its predictions may not accurately describe individual finite ecosystems. Here, we derive rigorous geometric bounds on the numerical ranges and spectra of Jacobian matrices that are valid for any finite number of species without assuming randomness. These bounds link long-term stability and short-term stability to the symmetric component of abundance-weighted interactions, and constrain the maximum oscillation frequency by the skew-symmetric component. Applied to random ensembles, the bounds also yield constraints on ensemble averages of long-term stability, short-term stability, and the maximum oscillation frequency in terms of standard RMT parameters. Using empirical data from marine food webs, we show that our bounds provide informative constraints on short-term stability and the maximum oscillation frequency even where RMT-based predictions fail. These results establish structural constraints on local ecosystem responses that complement RMT-based statistical predictions for large random ecosystems.
item.dc:creator: Koya Katayama, Sosuke Ito

item.title: Spatial effects of Kuramoto modeling on the power-grid frequencies
item.description: arXiv:2611.12132v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial coupling and heterogeneity can generate complex power-grid frequency dynamics. We investigate the contributions of spatial structure, intrinsic nonlinear dynamics, and external driving using the Kuramoto model (KM), with and without uncorrelated noise, and compare its predictions with real-grid measurements. We analyse one month of 100 ms frequency measurements from 16 Hungarian transmission-grid sites and simulate the KM on a 387-node transmission network and two-dimensional lattices. The measured power spectra exhibit two scaling regimes, with exponents of approximately 1.63 and 2.23. One-second frequency increments decorrelate rapidly, while correlations of their local inverse variance decay slowly, initially as a power law, $\tau^{-0.26(2)}$, up to 15 minutes. A superstatistical Gaussian mixture based on measured local variances captures much of the non-Gaussian increment distribution, but not the rare extreme events. We also estimate the non-stationary long-time frequency autocorrelation exponent. KM simulations on low-dimensional networks exhibit algebraically decaying autocorrelations and power spectra, consistent with the measurements and the Wiener-Khinchin relation in the steady state. On the heterogeneous transmission network, partial synchronization and frequency locking produce persistent spatial patterns and multi-peaked frequency distributions. However, neither deterministic KM dynamics nor independent Gaussian driving reproduces the measured spectra and increment statistics simultaneously. Moreover, empirical frequency fluctuations are largely shared across substations, whereas simulated fluctuations mainly reflect relative node motion. These findings suggest that spatially coupled nonlinear dynamics contribute to observed frequency fluctuations alongside external driving, including 15-minute power dispatches.
item.dc:creator: Krist\'of Benedek, Michelle T. Cirunay, Sangita Dutta, Attila Balogh, B\'alint Hartmann, G\'eza \'Odor

item.title: On transition probabilities for the ASEP on the half-line
item.description: arXiv:2611.12258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the asymmetric simple exclusion process on the half-line with particle insertion and no particle removal at the boundary. We point out that there exist two distinct multiple contour integral formulas for the transition probability between two finite particle configurations containing the same number of particles. We recall one of these formulas from the literature and prove a second, new formula by showing that it satisfies the evolution equation using a coordinate Bethe ansatz calculation and verify that the initial condition is implemented by the contour integrals. As an application we sum this formula over all final configurations and obtain an integral formula for the probability that the number of particles is conserved up to a given time. The proofs use symmetric rational functions and their properties together with contour deformations.
item.dc:creator: Alexandr Garbali, Cengiz Gazi, Jan de Gier, William Mead, Michael Wheeler

item.title: Resetting-based designated information distribution
item.description: arXiv:2611.12485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For a network of $n$ nodes under random gossip dynamics, we show that by introducing the additional resetting mechanism (with rate $\beta$) to a designated subset of $r$ nodes, the expected sum of all node values is asymptotically equal to $\tfrac{n}{r}$ times the sum of the initial values of the $r$ designated nodes, in the small-$\beta$ and long-time limit. We also analyze the convergence speed to this asymptotic state and provide an approximate high-probability confidence interval for the expected sum at finite time $t$ and finite $\beta$. Operationally, we propose a protocol that distributes the initial node values over the designated subset evenly (up to a prescribed precision), by appropriately turning on and off the resetting dynamics. Our work not only offers insights into classical problems such as distributed computing and network control, but also serves as a potential foundation for designing quantum algorithms that prepare desired states in quantum networks using only local operations.
item.dc:creator: Xiaojuan Ma, Yan Wang, Indranil Gupta

item.title: One-Particle Resonances and Eigenstate Thermalization in Periodic Free-Fermion Lattices
item.description: arXiv:2611.12701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study eigenstate fluctuations of the particle number in the nearest-neighbour free-fermion model on the periodic cubic lattice $(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^d$. For every fixed dimension, every particle number, every subvolume, and every normalized energy eigenstate, we prove a bound of order $NL^{d-1}$ for the particle-number variance. The corresponding eigenstate-thermalization estimate is of order $L^{d-1}/(N\eta^2)$ for fluctuations of relative size $\eta$. In particular, at positive particle density the bound decays as the inverse linear size. The proof decomposes the centered particle-number operator according to one-particle energy transfer and treats the zero- and nonzero-transfer components separately. The nonzero-transfer part is controlled by a sharp resonance bound, proved from Mann's theorem on relations among roots of unity, while the zero-transfer part is estimated by a Hilbert-Schmidt argument. These bounds are optimal in every dimension: the maximal nonzero-gap multiplicity has order $L^{d-1}$, and suitable many-body eigenstates realize matching variance lower bounds and show that the concentration bound cannot be improved in estimates uniform in the tolerance parameter.
item.dc:creator: Tristan Benoist, Vojkan Jak\v{s}i\'c, Claude-Alain Pillet, Anna Szczepanek, Cornelia Vogel

item.title: Global Asymptotics of a Toda Soliton Condensate with Random Scattering Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.12748v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a dense $N$-soliton condensate for the infinite Toda lattice in the limit $N \to \infty$. In contrast to previous mathematical studies of soliton gases where the norming constants are assumed to be deterministic or infinitesimal, we consider initial scattering data where both the discrete eigenvalues and the norming constants are independent random variables. The norming constants $\gamma_j$ are allowed to be arbitrarily large under a mild moment condition $\mathbb{E}[\gamma_j^\nu] < \infty$ ($\nu > 1$). Our main result is divided into two parts. First, we develop a probabilistic Riemann--Hilbert framework to show that the system self-averages: despite large, independent fluctuations in the initial data, the random Toda lattice variables converge deterministically to an effective continuum model at a polynomial rate $\mathcal{O}(N^{-\delta})$ for $0 < \delta < 1/2$. Second, by performing the Deift--Zhou nonlinear steepest descent analysis of the continuum problem, we obtain the complete leading-order macroscopic description of the lattice across the entire space-time plane. The solution decomposes into five distinct finite-gap regimes, characterized explicitly by modulated elliptic and genus-2 waves with an error of order $\mathcal{O}(1/\ln N)$. In contrast to the straight characteristic rays typical of standard soliton gas limits, the interfaces separating these five macroscopic regimes in the space-time plane are genuinely non-linear curves; in particular, the boundary of the modulated genus-2 region is completely non-linear. Finally, under our assumptions, we establish the Nonlinear Dispersion Relations for the Toda soliton condensate and prove that the macroscopic ensemble averages are determined by the soliton gas density of states.
item.dc:creator: Guido Mazzuca, Mateusz Piorkowski

item.title: An efficient classical algorithm for OTOCs in chaotic quantum dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.12773v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in individual instances of random quantum circuits has been proposed as a candidate for verifiable quantum advantage, and demonstrated to be hard for conventional classical algorithms such as tensor networks and Monte Carlo. Using insights from quantum chaos, we develop and implement a polynomial-time classical algorithm for the four-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and the eight-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in typical instances of one-dimensional (1D) quantum circuits. Our results demonstrate average-case classical tractability of estimating OTOCs in the sensitive regime where circuit-to-circuit fluctuations are large. Our algorithm organizes the OTOC into a rapidly converging series, where the leading term includes contributions from histories within permutation degrees of freedom in the replicated Hilbert space, and subleading terms arise from excursions outside this space. Although chaos is often viewed as an insurmountable barrier to classical simulation, our algorithm exploits a form of dephasing caused by chaos, which suppresses the subleading terms. We provide strong theoretical and numerical evidence to support this suppression. Further, we demonstrate that practical implementations of our algorithm estimate ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in 1D circuits with high accuracy, achieving higher signal-to-noise ratio at larger circuit depths compared to recent 2D experiments by Google. Extending our algorithm to higher dimensions, and resolving the status of quantum advantage in 2D OTOCs, remain open problems.
item.dc:creator: Yunchao Liu, Yihui Quek, Shreya Vardhan, Tianci Zhou

item.title: Shaking the causal tree: On the faithfulness and minimality assumptions beyond pairwise interactions
item.description: arXiv:2203.10665v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Higher-order mechanisms can make genuine causes invisible to causal discovery, but whether this reflects fine tuning or a structural limitation remains unclear. We prove, for a binary causal family, that the failure of faithfulness is not a measure-zero pathology: it persists for every nonzero coupling vector, even though every active edge remains causally minimal. Experiments with established causal-discovery methods show how this separation propagates into algorithm-dependent failures. A Partial Information Decomposition then identifies the lattice supports probed by faithfulness and minimality, placing the two premises at opposite ends of a single conditioning hierarchy. This exposes a two-sided obstruction: synergy can erase faithfulness, while redundancy can make the positive margin protecting minimality arbitrarily weak. Exact causal premises and practical discoverability can therefore point in different directions
item.dc:creator: Tiago Martinelli, Diogo O. Soares-Pinto, Francisco A. Rodrigues

item.title: Deriving Tsallis entropy from $q$-deformed Hamiltonian within a statistical mechanics framework
item.description: arXiv:2411.16757v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Tsallis entropy, which possesses $q$-additive property, is derived from the first principle employing the non-additive Hamiltonian or the $q$-deformed Hamiltonian with the canonical ensemble assumption in statistical mechanics. Here, the $q$-algebra and properties of $q$-deformed functions are extensively used throughout the derivation. Consequently, the thermodynamic quantities, e.g. internal energy and Helmholtz free energy, are derived and they inherently exhibit the $q$-additivity. From this intriguing connection between Tsallis entropy and the $q$-deformed Hamiltonian, the parameter $q$ encapsulates the intrinsic degree of $q$-additivity for the thermodynamic systems.
item.dc:creator: Paradon Krisut, Sikarin Yoo-Kong

item.title: Pilot-waves and copilot-particles: A nonstochastic approach to objective wavefunction collapse
item.description: arXiv:2506.08168v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We seek an extension to Schrodinger's equation that incorporates the macroscopic measurement-induced wavefunction collapse phenomenon. We find that a suitable hybrid between two leading approaches, the Bohm-de Broglie pilot-wave and objective collapse theories, accomplishes this goal in a way that is consistent with Born's rule. Our theory posits that the Bohmian particle is guided by the wavefunction and, conversely, the wavefunction gradually localizes towards the particle's position. As long as the particle can visit any state, as in a typical microscopic system, the localization effect does not favor any particular quantum state and, on average, the usual Schrodinger-like time evolution results. However, when the wavefunction develops spatially well-separated lobes, as would happen during a macroscopic measurement, the Bohmian particle can remain trapped in one lobe, which causes the wavefunction to eventually localizes. This proposed loss of ergodicity mechanism recasts one of the foundational postulate of quantum mechanics as a emergent feature and has important implications regarding the feasibility of large-scale quantum computing.
item.dc:creator: Axel van de Walle

item.title: Metastable phase separation and information retrieval in multicomponent liquids
item.description: arXiv:2509.10705v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Liquid mixtures can separate into phases with distinct composition. This phenomenon has recently come back to prominence due to its role in complex biological liquids, such as the cytoplasm, which contain thousands of components. For simple two-component mixtures phase-separated states are global free energy minima. However, local free energy minima, i.e., metastable states, are known to play a dominant role in complex systems with many components. For example, Hopfield neural networks can retrieve stored information from partial cues via relaxation to metastable states. Under what conditions can phase separated states be metastable, and what are the implications for information retrieval in multicomponent liquids? In this work we develop the general thermodynamic formalism of metastable phase separation. We then apply this formalism to an illustrative toy example inspired by recent experiments, binary mixtures with high-order interactions. Finally, as core application of the formalism, we study metastability in Hopfield liquids, a class of multicomponent mixtures capable of storing information on the composition of phases. We show that these phases can be nucleated from partial cues via metastable phase separation. Spatial simulations of liquids with a large number of components match our analytical solution. Our work suggests that complex biological mixtures can retrieve information through metastable phase separation.
item.dc:creator: Davide Marcato, Rodrigo Braz Teixeira, Izaak Neri, Pablo Sartori

item.title: Statistical Physics of Coding for the Integers
item.description: arXiv:2604.00858v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study a paradigm of coding for compression of the natural numbers via the zeta distribution and develop a statistical-mechanical interpretation, both in terms of Hagedorn systems and a Bose gas with energy levels given by logarithms of prime numbers. We also propose a simple coding scheme for the zeta distribution that nearly achieves the ideal code length. For block coding of vectors of natural numbers, we derive the micro-canonical entropy function and demonstrate its asymptotic linearity implying that its behavior is analogous to that of a Hagedorn system. We also derive the large deviations rate function, and provide a formula for the best coding parameter in the large deviations sense. We show that due the Hagedorn-type phase transition there is only partial equivalence of ensembles, due to the degeneration of the domain of the partition function.
item.dc:creator: Neri Merhav

item.title: Klein bottle ratio of two-dimensional ferromagnetic Potts models
item.description: arXiv:2604.00870v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The weakly first-order nature of the two-dimensional five-state ferromagnetic Potts model poses challenges for numerical study. Using density-matrix and tensor-network renormalization group methods, we investigate these transitions of the $q$-state Potts model via the Klein bottle ratio $g$ on original and dual lattices. Finite-size scaling of $g$ as a function of transverse system size $L_y$ accurately locates the critical points for $q = 3, 4, 5, 6$. We further examine the transfer-matrix spectra and entanglement entropy, extracting central charges through toroidal and Klein bottle boundary conditions. For $q = 5$, the extracted central charge ($c \approx 1.14811$) is close to the real part of the theoretical value $c_{5\text{-Potts}} = 1.1375 \pm 0.0211 i$ predicted by complex conformal field theories(CFTs). The observed drift in the scaling exponent $b$ effectively distinguishes the continuous transition from the weakly first-order regime. Furthermore, the extrapolated divergence of $g$ confirms the first-order character of the $q=5$ Potts model, while for the $q=4$ model, both the CFT-predicted eigenvalue distribution and the logarithmic corrections are numerically verified.
item.dc:creator: Zi-Han Wang, Li-Ping Yang

item.title: Genuine quantum scars in Floquet chaotic many-body systems
item.description: arXiv:2604.13164v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Unstable periodic orbits act as organizing structures for classical chaotic systems and underpin quantum scarring. Long known in single-particle systems, genuine quantum scars based on unstable periodic orbits have been recently extended to isolated many-body systems for time-independent Hamiltonians. Their fate under periodic driving, however, remains largely uncharted, challenged by the expectation that these systems should in general heat to infinite temperature. Here, we investigate how genuine scarring competes with the drive in a Floquet many-body system. Using chaotic spin chains, we demonstrate that Floquet states remain scarred in the high-frequency limit. Beyond this static correspondence, we uncover additional, driving-induced Floquet scars with no static analog. We construct a rich dynamical stability diagram with intermediate-frequency regimes of enhanced and quenched scarring, which we understand with a classical analysis of the Lyapunov exponent. Our results position Floquet systems as a natural platform for tuning the scarring behavior of quantum many-body systems.
item.dc:creator: Harald Schmid, Andrea Pizzi, Johannes Knolle

item.title: Mean-Field Theory for the Three-State Active Lattice Gas Model
item.description: arXiv:2604.22536v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a mean-field description including spatial structure for a simplified version of the three-state active matter model studied by Venzel et al. (Phys. Rev. E 110, 014109 (2024)). The resulting triangular lattice of coupled nonlinear differential equations are integrated numerically using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme. Starting from various ordered initial configurations, we probe the stability of the corresponding stationary states, revealing the presence of various high-density ordered structures in the density(\r{ho})-noise({\eta}) plane. The results are compared with Monte Carlo simulations of the simplified model, yielding, in certain cases, unexpected transitions between ordered configuration types.
item.dc:creator: Ana L. N. Dias, Ronald Dickman, Tiago Venzel Rosembach

item.title: Theory of melting lines with a variable enthalpy of fusion
item.description: arXiv:2605.17631v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conventional derivations of phase boundaries from the Clausius-Clapeyron (CC) relation often employ the constant latent heat approximation to maintain analytical functions for sublimation and boiling curves. To address the complex thermodynamics of the solid-liquid transition, we develop a two-phase analytical model by modifying the CC equation to account for a variable enthalpy of fusion along the melting line. Our framework incorporates recent theoretical and experimental progress showing that the ratio of the isobaric heat capacity to the thermal volume expansion coefficient in the solid state is a material constant correlating with the fusion enthalpy and the specific volumes of coexisting phases during melting. Differentiation of this modified CC relation in the low-pressure regime yields a second-order differential equation dictating the melting curve. By imposing appropriate boundary conditions, physically acceptable approximate parabolic solutions are derived. The parameters of these analytic functions are defined exclusively by fundamental thermophysical properties, including the bulk moduli, thermal expansion coefficients, specific volumes of the coexisting phases, and the isobaric heat capacity of the solid state. Rooted in solid-state anharmonicity, our derivation yields approximate parabolic scaling laws that corroborate a recent universal model derived from the Phonon Theory of Liquids [K. Trachenko, Phys. Rev. E 109, 034122 (2024)], supporting the universal parabolic nature of melting curves from a completely distinct theoretical foundation.
item.dc:creator: Anthony N. Papathanassiou

item.title: Finite-resolution exhaustive traversal of thermodynamic state spaces has divergent thermodynamic length
item.description: arXiv:2606.29751v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Resolving a prescribed multidimensional control window by a single continuous, serial scan is a task distinct from driving between fixed endpoints. We formulate this task as metric coverage at resolution $\eps$. Classical covering estimates, applied to a compact regular $d$-dimensional Riemannian window, give a required length of order at least $\eps^{1-d}$; local grid traversals attain the same exponent. When a physical friction tensor uniformly dominates the coverage metric, this geometric cost implies a necessary duration of order at least $\eps^{-2(d-1)}$ at fixed quadratic excess-work budget. Fixed-duration divergence refers to the slow-driving quadratic action and is not a claim about exact work outside that regime. A detailed-balance three-state process and an overdamped harmonic trap provide microscopic friction examples. For the trap, independently integrated Gaussian moment dynamics approach the quadratic prediction as the prescribed raster is slowed, while refinement at a controlled work budget increases scan duration. A quasi-uniform operational resolution floor cuts off the geometric divergence. Landau-response and van der Waals proxy metrics serve separately as prescribed diagnostic geometries: independent quadrature tests their coordinate- and protocol-dependent critical prefactors without asserting universal critical dissipation. Morton ordering supplies an ordering/connector benchmark with larger finite-resolution amplitudes. The resulting resource statements apply to exhaustive serial coverage, with metric, interpolation and driving assumptions specified explicitly.
item.dc:creator: Satori Tsuzuki

item.title: Bound state of a He-3 atom at free He-4 surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2608.27664v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum Monte Carlo simulations confirm the existence of a bound state of a single He-3 atom at a free superfluid He-4 surface in three dimensions, localized within a ~10-A thick low-density He-4 surface layer, with a binding energy of approximately 5 K with respect to vacuum. As the temperature is raised above ~ 1 K the He-3 atom leaves the surface to dissolve into the superfluid. The situation is entirely different in two dimensions, as the He-3 atom is excluded from the superfluid and no surface bound state exists. Results are also presented for the a He-3 atom binding to nanoscale size He-4 clusters adsorbed on weak substrates, a physical system that may allow for the observation of some of the physics predicted for extended surfaces. It is shown that a He-3 bound state localized at the perimeter of sufficiently small (a few tens of atoms) clusters exists not just on Cs, as previously reported, but on all alkali substrates.
item.dc:creator: Massimo Boninsegni

item.title: Mechanical modulation of the Gutenberg-Richter b-value in hierarchical fault networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.02541v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Gutenberg-Richter (G-R) law is seismology's most robust empirical regularity, yet a unified mechanical explanation for its slope-the b-value-remains a subject of ongoing debate. Here, we propose a framework suggesting that the b-value is mechanically modulated by the hierarchical architecture of fault networks. By coupling fracture mechanics with hierarchical network topology, we derive a generalized closed-form expression: b=\frac{3}{3+2\gamma}\frac{\log_{10}k}{\log_{10}q}. We further link these topological parameters to rate-and-state friction theory, illustrating that k and q can be mechanistically constrained by the competition between elastic stiffness, frictional healing, and energy dissipation. The empirical universality of b=1 may arise as the system balances these competing mechanisms, tending to reside near a mechanically balanced state (k=q). Furthermore, the dynamic decoupling of k and q under tectonic loading drives the system away from this critical state, providing a mechanical explanation for observed b-value anomalies. The stress-drop scaling exponent {\gamma} enters as a modulated perturbation about the constant-stress ({\gamma}=0) zeroth-order baseline: it shifts b only where source-scaling data independently constrain {\gamma} away from zero. By establishing a mechanistic connection between macroscopic statistical variations and microscopic mechanical processes, this framework may provide a new perspective for interpreting fault dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Bin Chen, Mingze Zhao, Puyu Cao

item.title: Origins of suppressed self-diffusion of nanoscale constituents of a complex liquid
item.description: arXiv:2404.17756v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding and ultimately controlling the transformations and properties of nanoscale systems, from proteins to synthetic nanomaterial assemblies, is limited by the inability to uncover their dynamics on their characteristic length and time scales. Here, we nevertheless demonstrate this ability using MHz X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) -- directly elucidating the characteristic microsecond-dynamics of density fluctuations of semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs), not only in a colloidal dispersion but, more importantly, in a liquid phase consisting of densely packed, yet mobile, NCs with no long-range order. We find the wavevector-dependent fluctuation rates in the liquid phase are suppressed relative to those in the colloidal phase and relative to observations of densely packed repulsive particles. We show that the suppressed rates are due to a substantial decrease in the self-diffusion of NCs, which we attribute to explicit attractive interactions. Using coarse-grained simulations, we find that the extracted shape and strength of the interparticle potential explains the stability of the liquid phase, in contrast to the gelation observed via XPCS in many other charged colloidal systems. This work opens the door to elucidating fast, condensed phase dynamics in complex fluids and other nanoscale soft matter, such as densely packed proteins and non-equilibrium self-assembly processes, in addition to designing microscopic strategies to avert gelation.
item.dc:creator: Christian P. N. Tanner, Vivian R. K. Wall, Mumtaz Gababa, Joshua Portner, Ahhyun Jeong, Matthew J. Hurley, Nicholas Leonard, Jonathan G. Raybin, James K. Utterback, Ahyoung Kim, Andrei Fluerasu, Yanwen Sun, Johannes Moeller, Alexey Zozulya, Wonhyuk Jo, Felix Brausse, James Wrigley, Ulrike Boesenberg, Jan-Etienne Pudell, Joerg Hallmann, Wei Lu, Roman Shayduk, Mohamed Youssef, Anders Madsen, David T. Limmer, Dmitri V. Talapin, Samuel W. Teitelbaum, Naomi S. Ginsberg

item.title: Computationally sufficient statistics for Ising models
item.description: arXiv:2602.12449v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learning Gibbs distributions using only sufficient statistics has long been recognized as a computationally hard problem. On the other hand, computationally efficient algorithms for learning Gibbs distributions rely on access to full sample configurations generated from the model. For many systems of interest that arise in physical contexts, expecting a full sample to be observed is not practical, and hence it is important to look for computationally efficient methods that solve the learning problem with access to only a limited set of statistics. We examine the trade-offs between the power of computation and observation within this scenario, employing the Ising model as a paradigmatic example. We show that the couplings of the model can be learned to a desired accuracy from statistics whose order grows linearly with the $\ell_1$ width of the model and only logarithmically with the inverse of the accuracy. In particular, for a fixed accuracy, the required order is proportional to the width. This allows us to infer the model's structure, using statistics whose order grows logarithmically with the inverse of the weakest coupling, and also to learn its magnetic fields. When the width and the accuracy are fixed, the running time is polynomial in the number of variables. We also discuss a setting where prior information about structure of the model is available and show that the learning problem can be solved efficiently with even more limited observational power.
item.dc:creator: Abhijith Jayakumar, Shreya Shukla, Marc Vuffray, Andrey Y. Lokhov, Sidhant Misra

item.title: Topology of the Fermi surface and universality of the metal-metal and metal-insulator transitions: $d$-dimensional Hatsugai-Kohmoto model as an example
item.description: arXiv:2602.13050v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The earlier theory \cite{Chitov:2025} of the quantum phase transitions related to the change of the Fermi Surface Topology (FST) is advanced. For such transitions the Fermi surface as a quantum critical manifold determined by the Lee-Yang zeros, the order parameter $\mathcal{P}$ as the $d$-volume of the Fermi sea, and the special FST universality class were introduced in \cite{Chitov:2025}. The exactly solvable Hatsugai-Kohmoto (HK) $d$-dimensional ($d=1,2,3$) model of interacting fermions is analyzed. We explore the relation between the Lee-Yang zeros, the Luttinger and the plateau (Oshikawa) theorems. The validity of the Luttinger theorem in the HK model is confirmed. It is shown that the order parameter $\mathcal{P}$ and the FST universality class describe the transitions between metal and band/Mott insulators, as well as the Lifshitz and van Hove gapless-to-gapless transitions. The gapless phases are established to be the ferromagnetic Fermi liquids (metals), where the quantum critical manifold is also a locus of ferromagnetic order with spontaneous breaking of the rotational symmetry occurring at $T=0$. In addition to the conventional paradigm with a continuous order parameter, we apply the homology theory to analyze the FST transitions. They are critical points of the Morse function. To quantify FST we use the Euler characteristic, which is calculated for each phase of the HK model. We claim that the FST universality class is robust with respect to interactions and other model details, under the condition that the conduction band function is smooth and the critical points are non-degenerate.
item.dc:creator: Gennady Y. Chitov

item.title: Scaling signatures of near-critical dynamics in large-scale human resting-state electrophysiology
item.description: arXiv:2602.17820v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: From 1/f noise to neuronal avalanches, evidence of scaling in brain activity has been increasingly linked to tuning to or near criticality. The concept of scaling is intimately related to the renormalization group (RG), in essence providing coarse-grained, simplified descriptions that generalize to classes of diverse physical systems. Following the RG idea, scaling laws have been reported in populations of spiking neurons at microscopic scales. Whether similar scaling principles govern large-scale neural activity in the human brain and how they relate to underlying neural physiology remains unresolved. Here, we analyze large-scale electrophysiological recordings (MEG) of human resting-state brain activity and apply a RG-inspired coarse-graining approach to track collective neural dynamics across spatial scales. We find that multiple observables exhibit robust scale-invariant behavior under coarse-graining: activity variance and correlations grow according to power laws, covariance eigenspectra follow a characteristic scaling relation, and neuronal avalanche statistics and scaling relationships are conserved. Using an analytically tractable neural network model with parameters inferred from data, we show that the observed scaling signatures arise close to, but slightly below, criticality, and that the scaling exponents can be modulated by network inhibitory drives. These findings demonstrate that RG-inspired scaling analysis can uncover signatures of critical dynamics in non-invasive human electrophysiology and suggest a principled route toward estimating excitation-inhibition balance from large-scale brain recordings.

item.title: Noise-induced suppression of MPO truncation errors in noisy random circuits and Lindbladian dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2603.20400v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how matrix product operator (MPO) truncation errors evolve when simulating two setups: (1) one-dimensional (1D) Haar-random circuits under either depolarizing noise or amplitude-damping noise, and (2) 1D Lindbladian dynamics of a non-integrable quantum Ising model under either depolarizing or amplitude-damping noise. We first show that the average purity of the system density matrix relaxes to a steady value on a timescale that scales inversely with the noise rate. We find that truncation errors generated at earlier steps are approximately exponentially contracted by the subsequent noisy evolution, both with system size $N$ and with the evolution depth $t$, while the cumulative error results from the competition between this contraction and newly injected compression errors. We complement the local-circuit numerics with a solvable global random-unitary model in which the same channel-dependent factor governs the mean-squared contraction of traceless errors and transient mean purity. Its exact finite-$N$ results capture the weak-noise contraction rates and the non-unital stationary-purity trend. Combining the resulting $L_2$ error characterization with the observed late-time $L_1/L_2$ conversion yields an empirical estimate of the $L_1$ truncation error that can be exponentially tighter in $N$ than the generic rank-based bound, particularly for non-unital noise. Together, these results provide empirical evidence that MPO simulation algorithms may efficiently sample from the output of 1D noisy random circuits [setup (1)] with an arbitrary number of circuit layers, and from the steady state of 1D Lindbladian dynamics [setup (2)].
item.dc:creator: Zhi-Yuan Wei, Joel Rajakumar, Jon Nelson, Jens Eisert, Daniel Malz, Michael J. Gullans, Alexey V. Gorshkov

item.title: Quantum Charge-4e Superconductivity and Possible Deconfined Pseudocriticality in the Attractive SU(4) Hubbard Model
item.description: arXiv:2604.14289v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unlike conventional charge-2e superconductors, a charge-4e superconductor exhibits long-range coherence of electron quartets rather than Cooper pairs. Clear zero-temperature realizations of charge-4e superconductivity remain rare. Here, we investigate the zero-temperature phase diagram of the attractive SU(4) Hubbard model with numerically exact, large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations overcoming major technical hurdles. We identify both charge-2e and charge-4e superconducting phases. Upon increasing interaction, charge-2e long-range order vanishes, while charge-4e correlations remain robust and converge with system size, establishing a quartet-condensed phase. Interestingly, across the charge-2e--charge-4e transition, single electrons remain gapped, while charge-2e correlations exhibit an effective anomalous dimension substantially exceeding the conventional O(6) Landau theory prediction. These features motivate a fractionalized framework in which the physical charge-2e order parameter is a composite field coupled to an emergent non-Abelian gauge structure. We formulate an Sp(4) gauge-Higgs theory associating the charge-2e and charge-4e states with Higgs and confined phases, respectively. A one-loop analysis of an SU($N_f$) generalization exhibits a fixed-point collision, motivating deconfined pseudocriticality as a possible interpretation of the observed scaling. Our results establish charge-4e superconductivity as a bona fide zero-temperature phase, provide a simple model for future studies in a numerically exact framework, and suggest an unconventional route to superconducting criticality.
